Hi.

Ok, first thing I observe when I compare the two files, is that
'GSM123182.cel' is of file format v4 (binary) and 'GSM123184.cel' is
of file format v3 (ASCII). I then note that the ASCII file works, but
not the binary. I also note that it is not only then chip type that
is not correct, but all of the CEL header is blank. I have never
heard of something similar before. Have the binary CEL files been
converted from ASCII-to-binary by some tool?

If you could zip the two CEL files and make the available to me
somewhere so that I can download them, I could also have a look at
them.

Comment: You do indeed want to work with binary files (since ASCII is
slower and more memory-hungry to work with), although if you do for
instance quantile normalization on ASCII CEL files, the normalized
data is stored as binary CEL files, so you can "live with" having raw
data in the ASCII format.

/Henrik

Ok, both files are indeed in ASCII file format. The 'affxparser' is
using the Affymetrix Fusion SDK library internally. The latter does
parse all CEL/CDF file formats released by Affymetrix and since it is
used in many other software by many other users, we are rather
confident that it does the right thing, especially when it comes to
the common CEL and CDF formats.

This is the problem. If you look at the two CEL files in a text
editor on a non-Windows system or in a text editor that is not written
by Microsoft, you will see that 'GSM123182.cel' have extra carriage
returns that should not be there between every row. You can also see
this like this:

> readChar("GSM123182.cel", n=30)
[1] "[CEL] Version=3 [HEADER"
> readChar("GSM123184.cel", n=30)
[1] "[CEL] Version=3 [HEADER] "

Note the difference. There is an extra ' ' in the former. I
strongly suspect that this has happened because either i) those files
were downloaded via FTP in a non-binary mode (classical mistake) or
ii) someone have edited those files manually (most likely on an old
Mac OS v9 or before, cf http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newline).

You will need to remove all those errounous carriage returns in those
files, because as it is now, those CEL files does not comply with the
defined file format. Be care to backup your files so you keep the
originals in case something goes wrong while correcting the files.
You might be able to do something like:

library(aroma.affymetrix);
mkdirs("fixed");
pathname <- "GSM123184.cel";
raw <- readBin(con=pathname, what="raw", n=file.info(pathname)$size);
raw2 <- raw[raw != charToRaw(" ")];
pathname2 <- file.path("fixed", basename(pathname));
writeBin(con=pathname2, raw2);
hdr <- readCelHeader(pathname2);

Thanks Henrik,

You nailed the problem (the extra \r in the faulty files). So we used
a little script (outside R) to get all the files fixed in batch mode.
It turned out that among 5896 cel files, only a handful (31) are
affected. We also had to filter out the [MODIFIED] section in the cel
files since they do contain valid (maybe) \r\r markers.

Here is the little bash script that does the job, for future
reference.

ls | xargs -n 1 bash -c 'perl -ne "if (1../\[MODIFIED\]/) { if (/\\r\\r
$/) { print \"`echo $1`\n\"; exit() }}" $1' -- | xargs -n 1 perl -
i.bak -pe 's/\r\r$//'

Now we are happily on the QN part. It has been 20 hours since the
processing started, and now it is running on the 4200th chip. The
memory usage is about 560M so far, very impressive.

I will keep you posted on the results.

Dong

and the signal from one array in memory at any time. You'll find all

RMA), if that is what you plan, the processing time is exponential(?)
in the number of probes. This is something that have bitten a few
processing exon array data using the default Affymetrix CDF. You can
find studies on this on Page "Optimization (Speed, file space & RAM)":

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/optimization-speed-file-space-ram

Hello Henrik,

Do you ever rest and not respond so quickly? :-) Just kidding.

Once the QN is finished, we will do the RMAPLM on it.

Just for reference. We ran the same steps on about 1500 arrays last
week. The QN took about 10 hours, and the RMAPLM took about 20
hours. The memory usage during the calculation was very constant at
around 500MB.

The only wish I have is for R to take advantage of the multi-core/
multi-CPU capability at a more fundamental level. Right now it is
using only 1 CPU 100% while the rest of the CPUs are idling. I could
try using the fork package, but with the stringent requirement of
directory structure right now, it might be too messy.

Dong

This took a bit longer than I anticipated, but it still do the job.
After each chunk you should see an estimate of ETA and how much time
spent for reading, fitting, and writing. Unfortunately, writing takes
quite some time, but what percentage do you get?

Also, it is typically much faster to process the data on a local drive
than over a file network, but I'm not sure if you've got the option to
do it locally.

>
> So is there a way to have the RmaPlm pick up from where it left off?
> Or do we need to start from scratch? I found that in the plmData
> folder there are a lot of processed data files already.

It picks up where it ended. In each chunk, first the probe affinities
are saved, then the chip effects array by array. The fit() function
look at the last array to decide what units need to be fitted, e.g. if
the R session is interrupted while writing, it will refit that whole
last chunk.

I've used the above many times; for instance running it on one
machine, then interrupt R in order to move the processing to another.

> spent for reading, fitting, and writing. Unfortunately, writing takes
> quite some time, but what percentage do you get?
>
> Also, it is typically much faster to process the data on a local drive
> than over a file network, but I'm not sure if you've got the option to
> do it locally.

Forgot to mention, there is also an argument 'ram=1' that fit() takes
- it is a "scale" factor and if you set 'ram' > 1, more units are
fitted per chunk (using more memory of course), which could save you
some of the I/O overhead.

/Henrik

>

> > Or do we need to start from scratch? I found that in the plmData
> > folder there are a lot of processed data files already.

> are saved, then the chip effects array by array. The fit() function
> look at the last array to decide what units need to be fitted, e.g. if
> the R session is interrupted while writing, it will refit that whole
> last chunk.
>
> I've used the above many times; for instance running it on one
> machine, then interrupt R in order to move the processing to another.
>

On Feb 18, 2008 9:33 AM, Dong Fu <dongf...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

>
> Does the same idea apply to the Quantile Normalization part? I saw
> there is a folder called probeData with a subfolder related to QN
> inside.

Yes, with a small disclaimer. So, the QN is done using a two-pass
scan of the data. In the first scan, the target/baseline distribution
is identified. This roughly "sums" the arrays and saves the "average"
in a target distribution file. So, if R is interrupted during this
first pass, it has to be redone all over. In the second pass, each
array is normalized to the target distribution, i.e. it is a
single-array normalization method at this stage. Any arrays already
normalized will be skipped. An array is considered normalized if
there exist an output file (the probeData/ one you refer to). Now to
the catch, the output data is current saved in two lines of code:

createFrom(this, filename=pathname, path=NULL, verbose=less(verbose));
updateCel(pathname, intensities=x);

The first one, createFrom(), creates an empty CEL file and the second
one writes the normalized data to that file. I have taken greate care
of making the first one "atomic", i.e. it either returns a valid CEL
file or not. Now, if the R session is interrupted after createFrom()
but before updateCel() [in affxparser] is complete, the result will be
a CEL files only partially populated. updateCel() is rather fast so
the risk is not that big, but still there.

It is on my todo list to make the above two calls as one "atomic"
call, i.e. either you get a CEL file with normalized data or you
don't. In the meanwhile, you can delete the last CEL file written in
the probeData/...,QN/ directory to be on the safe side.

> On the other hand, I will do the RmaBackgroundCorrection
> before doing the QN part this time, so maybe I need to redo this
> anyway.

Yes, I remember you question on how well aroma.affymetrix replicates
rma(). If you to a small-set comparison, I would be great if you
could share your findings here.

>
> So if I did not get to save the results of the CelSet loading from
> ds <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("myDataSet", chipType="HG-U133A"),
> do I also need to load them again?

I'm not sure what you mean by "save" here, but I might guess.
Basically the 'ds' object, which is of class AffymetrixCelSet, holds a
list of AffymetrixCelFile objects which each holds a pathname to the
CEL file (plus some other minor fields). That is all. The above
fromName() static method call will locate the CEL set and scan the
directory for CEL files and rebuild this structure. Since you have
5000+ arrays, this might take a substantial time for you, is that
right? In that case, you can use the file cache mechanism to do
something like this:

force <- FALSE;
key <- list(method="fromName", class="AffymetrixCelSet",
name="myDataSet", tags=NULL, chipType="HG-U133A");
dirs <- "myCacheDir";
ds <- loadCache(key, dirs=dirs);
if (force || is.null(ds)) {
ds <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("myDataSet", chipType="HG-U133A");
saveCache(ds, key=key, dirs=dirs);
}

This will cache the result in getCachePath(dirs=dirs) and you don't
have to worry about where you save it and what file name you use. the
(key, dirs) pair makes it unique.

Basically, I could add a 'force=TRUE' argument to fromName() and put
everything inside to do exactly that - this is what is done in many
places where a method is computational expensive. But I first have to
see if there are any side effects, before I do that.

>
> I will remember to save more often all the intermediate results as
> they all take a long while to generate.

You can also load normalized data directly by specifying the data set tags, e.g.

csN <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("myDataSet", tags="QN", chipType="HG-U133A");

and process from there.
